opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've been saying this for a while, so in some sense it's already obvious to me. But I think the broader community will come around fairly soon, for a simple reason: we're running into the limits of what you can do by scaling up large language models trained on text.

LLMs are very useful. They manipulate language extremely well, and that fools us into thinking they're more intelligent than they are. But language is a low-bandwidth, highly compressed representation of the world. A four-year-old child has taken in more data through vision alone than the biggest LLMs have seen in text. Most of what we know, and almost everything animals know, has nothing to do with language. It's about how the physical world works: intuitive physics, object permanence, causality, the consequences of your actions.

So if you want systems that can operate in the real world, like a domestic robot, a self-driving car that learns to drive in twenty hours the way a teenager does, or an assistant that can actually plan, you need systems that can predict what will happen in the world, and in particular what will happen as a result of their own actions. That's what a world model is. With a world model you can plan: you search for a sequence of actions that optimizes an objective, instead of autoregressively generating one token after another and hoping it works out.

Why the next year or so? Two things are happening at once. First, people are seeing diminishing returns. We've basically run out of high-quality text on the internet, and the gains from more data and more compute are getting smaller. You can patch things with chain-of-thought, reasoning tricks and tool use, but those are band-aids on an architecture that fundamentally doesn't understand the physical world, doesn't have persistent memory, and can't really reason or plan.

Second, the alternative is starting to work. We've had a lot of progress with joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, where you don't try to predict every pixel, which is hopeless because the world is not fully predictable. Instead you learn an abstract representation and make predictions in that space. Systems like V-JEPA trained on video are beginning to show they can learn something like intuitive physics and be used for planning in robotics. Once people see these systems doing things LLMs simply cannot do, such as zero-shot planning for a robot arm in an environment it hasn't seen, the shift becomes hard to ignore.

So my prediction is that within a few years, nobody in their right mind will use generative autoregressive LLMs as the core of an intelligent system the way we do today. They'll still be around as the interface for language, but the core will be something else, and I think by around 2027 that will be pretty clear to most people in the field, and certainly to industry, because that's where the next wave of applications will come from.

r001.rationale: The response connects world models to real-world robotics and says robotic demonstrations may make the shift hard to ignore, but it does not clearly attribute the growing recognition specifically to efforts to make robots useful.

r002.rationale: It predicts that the need for a shift will be clear by around 2027, but does not distinguish that recognition from whether a working solution will exist by then.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I don't know that I ever put a precise date on it, but the reason I think the shift is going to become obvious fairly soon is that the limitations of the current paradigm are becoming impossible to ignore.

Look, LLMs are trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text. That works remarkably well for language because text is discrete, it's low-dimensional in a sense, and we have enormous amounts of it. But the real world is not text. The real world is continuous, high-dimensional, noisy, and most of the information in it is irrelevant to whatever you're trying to do. If you try to predict every pixel of a video the way you predict the next word, you fail. The system spends all of its capacity on details that are fundamentally unpredictable, like the exact shape of leaves moving in the wind, and it learns nothing useful about the underlying structure of the scene.

So what do you need instead? You need a system that learns an abstract representation of the state of the world, and then learns to predict how that state evolves, in representation space, as a consequence of actions. That's what a world model is. It's what allows a child to understand intuitive physics by ten months without anyone labeling anything. It's what allows a teenager to learn to drive in twenty hours. We can't do either of those with current AI systems, and it's not for lack of compute or data. It's an architectural problem.

Now, why do I think this becomes obvious on a relatively short timescale? Because the industry has bet enormous amounts of money on the idea that scaling LLMs gets you to human-level intelligence, and the returns are visibly flattening. People are starting to notice that these systems still can't plan reliably, still can't reason in a way that's grounded in the physical world, still hallucinate, and that bolting on more tokens and more test-time compute gives you incremental improvements, not a qualitative change. Meanwhile, the people who actually need AI in the physical world, robotics, autonomous systems, anything that has to act rather than talk, are discovering that language models just don't give them what they need.

And in parallel, the alternative is starting to work. Self-supervised approaches that learn representations by prediction in latent space rather than reconstructing inputs, the JEPA family of architectures and things like it, are showing that you can learn useful models of the world from video, and that those models support planning. Once you have a few convincing demonstrations of a system that learns from observation, builds a predictive model, and uses it to plan a sequence of actions to achieve a goal, the contrast with what LLMs can do will be stark.

So my view is that we're going to see a convergence of frustration with the current approach and visible progress on the alternative, and when those two things happen at the same time, the field moves. I've been wrong about timing before, I'll admit that. But I'm not wrong about the direction. The future of AI is not autoregressive token prediction. It's systems that understand the world, have persistent memory, can reason, and can plan. And that requires world models.

r001.rationale: The response says people working on robotics and other physical-world systems are discovering that language models do not meet their needs, contributing to recognition of the need for a different approach.

r002.rationale: It discusses when the shift may become obvious and mentions possible demonstrations, but it does not clearly distinguish recognition by early 2027 from having a working solution by then.

astra-6.text:
I think it will become obvious because we’ll keep running into the same limitations. A system can be extraordinarily fluent in language and still have a very poor understanding of what happens when it acts in the world. If you want a robot to help you around the house, it has to predict the consequences of its actions, deal with uncertainty, and plan. Producing plausible text does not, by itself, give you those capabilities.

What I mean by a world model is a system that learns how the world works well enough to predict how a situation might evolve, including in response to an action. It doesn’t have to predict every detail. It has to capture the things that matter for the task. Then you can use that model to evaluate possible actions before executing them.

So early 2027 is not some magical deadline. The prediction is that, as people push AI toward more demanding tasks in the physical world, the gap between linguistic competence and reliable action will become increasingly difficult to ignore. That will make the need for world models much more apparent.

r001.rationale: It says that pushing AI toward demanding physical-world tasks, including robots that help at home, will make the gap between language ability and reliable action harder to ignore and the need for world models more apparent.

r002.rationale: It frames early 2027 as when the need will become apparent, but does not distinguish that recognition from having a working solution by then.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think by then it will be clear that scaling language models alone doesn’t solve the problems we need to solve for intelligent systems in the real world. They’re very useful, but producing plausible text is different from understanding how the world evolves and predicting the consequences of your actions.

Take a domestic robot. You can give it an instruction, but it still has to figure out what to do when it encounters a situation it has never seen before. It needs some internal model that lets it predict: if I take this action, what happens next? Then it needs to use those predictions to plan a sequence of actions toward a goal.

That’s what I mean by a world model. It doesn’t necessarily predict every pixel of the future. It should predict in an abstract representation, keeping the information that matters for the task and ignoring details that are unpredictable or irrelevant.

Early 2027 is not some magical deadline. The point is that as we push toward robots and systems that can reliably carry out tasks, those missing capabilities will become increasingly difficult to ignore. Language can help you communicate a plan. It is not, by itself, a substitute for learning how the world works.

r001.rationale: The response says that as efforts push toward robots and systems that reliably carry out tasks, the missing capabilities will become harder to ignore.
